Learning to Learn
Learning is a continuous process that begins at birth and continues until death; it is the process
through which we use our experience to deal with new situations and to develop relationships.
As a concept, it involves far more than thinking as it incorporates the whole personality – senses,
feelings, intuition, beliefs, values and will. If we do not have the will to learn, we will not learn
and if we have learned, we are actually changed in some way. If the learning makes no
difference it can have very little significance beyond being random ideas that float through our
consciousness.
Learning to learn is the ability to pursue and persist in learning, to organise one‟s own learning
by the effective management of time and information, both individually and in groups. This
competence includes awareness of one‟s learning process and needs, identifying available
opportunities, and the ability to overcome obstacles in order to learn successfully. This
competence means gaining, processing and assimilating new knowledge and skills as well as
seeking and making use of guidance. Learning to learn helps learners to build on prior learning
and life experiences in order to use and apply knowledge and skills in a variety of contexts.
There are four pillars of learning: Learning to know, learning to do, learning to be and learning
to live to live together.
A competency based curriculum has the following strengths:
1. Learner-focused
The focus should be less on the school and the system and more on the education and the learner.
The curriculum should be responsive and relevant to learners and enable flexibility for teachers –
who are designers of learning opportunities – to enable them to meet the diverse needs of the
students.
2. Focus on Competencies
More focus should be directed to competencies and less on content. The goal should be the
appropriate application of knowledge, and not necessarily just its acquisition. This kind of
curriculum enables the creation of meaningful connections within and among subject areas by
focusing on competencies. Subjects/subjects/disciplines will continue to be taught and will be the
vehicle through which literacy, numeracy and other competencies are developed over time.
3. Opportunities for Local Decision Making and Greater Depth of Study
Prescriptive curricula with limited flexibility should be avoided, as should programs that have
fewer learning outcomes. The goal is to enable greater flexibility at the local level. Teachers will
have autonomy in implementing the curriculum while teaching.
4. Balance Between Formative and Summative Assessment
Too much focus on summative assessment should be avoided. A range of assessment that
focuses on the development of student learning outcomes, cross-curricular competencies, and
literacy and numeracy should be adopted.
26
Engaged, Empowered & Ethical Citizens
Basic Education Curriculum Framework                             Nurturing Every Learner’s Potential
5. Digitally Based
The design of the curriculum within a collaborative digital application enables it to be improved
continuously and supports learning with flexible timing and pacing through a range of learning
environments.
6. Collaborative and Co-development Models
Collaboration by all stakeholders in the curriculum design should be the norm. Co-creation of the
curriculum with partners and stakeholders taps into local expertise to enhance its design and
development. Content delivery will be flexible and exploratory.
7. Synchronous Development
Sequential development needs to be replaced with synchronous development. An integrated
approach to develop programmes of study, assessments, and learning and teaching resources
supports a common approach that encourages interdisciplinary learning.
Subjects
These are the subjects taught at various levels of the education. For example, English,
Mathematics, Science and Technology. Subjects are the means through which the key
competencies, values and knowledge will be taught across all levels of learning. However, they
are not static and may change to address the ever changing needs of society.
Organization of Basic Education
Basic Education will be organized into three (3) levels: Early Years Education, Middle School
Education and Senior School. Figure 2 presents a summary of the structural model.
27
Engaged, Empowered & Ethical Citizens
Basic Education Curriculum Framework                             Nurturing Every Learner’s Potential
Figure 2: Basic Education Structural Model
Early Years Education
This shall comprise two years of pre-primary and three years of lower primary school education.
28
Engaged, Empowered & Ethical Citizens
Basic Education Curriculum Framework                               Nurturing Every Learner’s Potential
Figure 3: Early Years Education Structural Model
Learning Outcomes for Early Years Education
By the end of early years‟ education, the learner should be able to:
1. Demonstrate basic literacy and numeracy skills for learning.
2. Communicate appropriately using verbal and/or non-verbal modes in a variety of contexts.
3. Demonstrate appropriate etiquette in social relationships.
4. Apply creativity and critical thinking skills in problem solving.
5. Explore the immediate environment for learning and enjoyment.
6. Practice hygiene, nutrition, sanitation, safety skills to promote health and wellbeing.
7. Demonstrate the acquisition of emotional, physical, spiritual, aesthetic and moral
development for balanced living.
8. Demonstrate appreciation of the country's rich and diverse cultural heritage for harmonious
co-existence.
9. Apply digital literacy skills for learning and enjoyment.
29
Engaged, Empowered & Ethical Citizens
Basic Education Curriculum Framework                                Nurturing Every Learner’s Potential
Pre-primary Education
All learners are expected to begin their education at this level. It is a two year programme.
Subjects for Pre-primary (Two Years)
1.   Language Activities
2.   Mathematical Activities
3.   Environmental Activities
4.   Psychomotor and Creative Activities
5.   Religious Education Activities
NB: Digital literacy and pertinent and contemporary issues will be integrated across all Subjects.
Essence Statements for the Pre-primary Curriculum
Language Activities
Language is an important tool for facilitating learning as children use it to interact with their
immediate environment. It is a medium of communication and a critical component of
socialization as it equips learners with skills that are necessary for listening and speaking as well
as developing literacy skills. Language acquisition at the formative level of human development
is based on several theoretical frameworks attributed to a number of early childhood specialists
and theorists such as Tricia (2004).
The essence of this activity area is to develop oral, reading readiness and writing readiness
competencies in order to lay the foundation for language acquisition. In pre-primary education,
the medium of instruction is the language of the catchment area. The aim of teaching language
activities at pre-primary school level is to enable learners to express themselves fluently and to
assist them to improve the listening ability, concentration, understanding and memory.
Mathematical Activities
Mathematical activities are important for laying a firm foundation for logical thinking and
problem solving. Learning mathematics at pre-primary level empowers children to engage in
basic analysis of problems and development of appropriate solutions in day to day life. It
enhances logical and critical thinking, accuracy and problem solving. During the early childhood
stage of development, learners are more engaged when using manipulative (carbonneau et al,
201; Cocket and Kilgour, 2015). Similarly, Piaget and Bruner attest that children at this level use
hands-on manipulation to physically arrive at a mathematical solution.
Pre-primary mathematics curricula should therefore comprise learning basic mathematical
concepts through manipulation of concrete objects and not abstract knowledge. Activities at this
level form a firm foundation for the acquisition of competencies in classification, number and
measurement skills.
Environmental Activities
30
Engaged, Empowered & Ethical Citizens
Basic Education Curriculum Framework                               Nurturing Every Learner’s Potential
Environmental activities entail the relationship between human beings and their environment.
These activities enable the child to develop positive relationships, appreciate the surrounding
environment and cultural heritage, develop observation and discovery skills, and acquire life
skills required to ensure safety in their environment. The curriculum must therefore offer
opportunities for the children to explore the environment around them in order to acquire
knowledge and skills that form the foundation for further learning. Exploration of the
environment allows unlimited opportunities for children to learn and satisfy their curiosity and
makes learning more fun for them.
The essence of environmental activities at the pre-primary level is to develop social,
experimentation and discovery, personal hygiene and safety skills among the children. Nature
study activities are best learnt through the inquiry method which includes simple
experimentation and observation. Social activities deal with acquisition of values and attitudes
which aid in the holistic development of an individual, while safety activities mainly deal with
life skills that ensure children remain safe and are not exposed to risks that may endanger their
lives.
Psychomotor and Creative Activities
Psychomotor and creative activities at pre-primary level enable learners to develop both fine and
gross motor skills which are necessary for the control and co-ordination of different parts of the
body. These activities enhance exploration and development of personal talents and skills as well
as appreciation of their cultural heritage.
Pre-primary physical and creative curriculum comprises play and learning activities through
which children exercise their bodies thereby facilitating blood and oxygen circulation for healthy
and strong growth and development as well creative activities through which children develop
their fine motor skills, imagination and creativity thereby developing their talents.
Religious Activities
Children need to participate in activities that integrate religion and moral values. Teachers should
help children to appreciate people of different religious backgrounds and to differentiate right
and wrong at an early age so they can grow up as upright members of the society. Children need
to be introduced to such values at an early age. Youniss et al (1999) found that the importance of
religion was consistently and positively associated with engaging in service activities. It is
therefore important to emphasize religious education in schools in order to instil acceptable
religious and moral values in young children.
Religious Education Activities at pre-primary level comprise learning about the supernatural
being (God). The aim of moral and religious activities at pre-school level is to develop awareness
and appreciation of the generosity, love and care of God in all He has created, and to enable
children to acquire the qualities of sharing, respect, kindness, getting along with others.
Lower Primary
31
Engaged, Empowered & Ethical Citizens
Basic Education Curriculum Framework                               Nurturing Every Learner’s Potential
The learners from pre-primary 2 will join lower primary in grade 1 at about 6 years of age and
spend 3 years in this part of Early Years Education before exiting to middle school at the end of
grade 3.
Subjects
The following will be the Subjects in lower primary
1.   Literacy
2.   Kiswahili Language Activities/Kenya Sign Language for learners who are deaf
3.   English Language Activities
4.   Indigenous Language Activities
5.   Mathematical Activities
6.   Environmental Activities
7.   Hygiene and Nutrition Activities
8.   Religious Education Activities
9.   Movement and Creative Activities
NB:
 ICT will be a learning tool in all areas.
 Pertinent and contemporary issues will be mainstreamed in all Subjects.
Essence Statements for Lower Primary
Literacy
Literacy is the ability to read, write and use language proficiently. According to UNESCO,
literacy is a basic human right. Literacy as a subject addresses the ability of the learner to make
meaning of letters and sounds thus making sense of written codes. It shall be taught in the first
language of the learner. At this foundational level, literacy aims at equipping the learner with
basic skills in reading and writing to aid in all other Subjects. It will assist the learner to
communicate with others as well as promote learning to learn.
Indigenous Language Ac

LIFE SKILLS EDUCATION
GRADE 7
ESSENCE STATEMENT
Life Skills Education is the study of the abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour
that
enable individuals to deal effectively with the demands and challenges of
everyday life.
It aims at enhancing the knowledge on and appreciation of oneself, the need to
value and promote good interpersonal skills, as well as improving the quality of
decisiveness in day-to-day life.
The need for the development and application of life skills is supported by
Vygotsky’s social-cultural development theory that presupposes that learning takes
place when learners interact with each other. Learners negotiate meanings with
people in the environment and achieve their goals by interacting with teachers,
peers, materials and the atmosphere embedded in the context.
CONT…..
LSE is anchored on Article 10 of the Constitution of Kenya 2010 which
prescribes the national values and principles that need to be inculcated into
all Kenyans. The third national goal of education, together with the Kenya
Vision 2030 recognize the contribution of LSE in promoting individual
development and self-fulfilment. Further, the National Education Sector
Plan (NESP 2018- 2022) which builds on successes and challenges of
previous sectoral plans, champions for a value-based education system,
and the need to transmit life skills, principles and values for personal,
social and economic development.
LSE equips the learners with psychosocial competencies and interpersonal
skills that enable them to make informed decisions, think creatively and
critically, communicate effectively, build healthy relationships, empathize
with others and manage their lives healthily and productively. The subject
moves beyond providing information to the development of the whole
individual.
GENERAL LEARNING OUTCOMES
By the end of the Junior Secondary School level, the learner
should be able to:
a) Possess a sense of self-understanding and self-worth for
personal holistic development.
b) Develop and maintain responsible interpersonal relationships
for harmonious living in society.
c) Make informed and appropriate decisions in life.
d) Exemplify values and positive attitudes while in school and
society.

challenges of everyday life.

Strand: Principles of Dharma

Specific learning outcome: describe the fundamental Principles of Dharma for knowledge in the four faiths.
Key Inquiry Question: Why is it important to learn principles of Dharma?
Learning Resources: Scriptures, Digital resources (Authenticated Online), Library, Magazines, Posters, Models,
Manilla papers, Pictures and photographs, Newspaper cuttings
HRE Course Books.
Organisation of Learning: learners will be organised in pairs, the learning will take place in class.
Introduction: Teacher reviews the previous lesson by asking key inquiry questions to focus learning and probe for
deeper thinking. Teacher introduces the lesson by playing a song relevant to the theme.
LESSON DEVELOPMENT
Step 1: Learners buzz on the meaning of fundamental principles; each pair give their definition; the
teacher and other learners give their comments. Learners note key points using a digital device/ write
in their exercise books.
 Core competence of Learning to Learn: will be enhanced as they learn from each other and note
down key points on the fundamental Principles of Dharma.
 The value of Responsibility: will be developed as learners research using prescribed authentic sites
and apply the Principles of Dharma in their lives.
 PCI; Positive Discipline: as learners discuss in groups the importance of Principles of Dharma in
their lives and listening attentively.
Step 2:
In pairs learners read fundamental principles from Sanatan faith and outline lessons learnt from the
principles, the teacher gives more inputs and guidance as the learners air their views/opinions.
The core competence of learning to learn is enhanced as learners outline lessons learnt from the
fundamental principles.
The value of unity is demonstrated as learners work in pairs and report their findings as a team
Performing Arts: as learners perform skits and create games on the Principles of Dharma.
Step 3:
Learners read fundamental principles or use a digital device;
The teachers ask learner’s questions on the values and life skills derived from those
principles.
Learners share with the class how the values help them to relate with each other at home
school and the community, the teacher will involve learners in the learning process by
calling them out by their names, provoke deeper thinking and keep learners focused by
asking more questions to make learning interesting,
Core competence; Citizenship: learners will develop communication skills as they visit places of worship and interact
with resource person(s) to gain insight on the application of Principles of Dharma. They will also develop an active
community life as they visit homes of elderly, orphanages, and animal shelters around them.
Value: respect for self and others is enhanced as learners exercise self-control and live responsibly.
PCI; Environmental Issues: learners will develop skills on human and animal welfare issues as they visit animal
shelters and homes for the elderly.
Extended Activity: At home discuss with your parents on how to relate with members of other communities, elders,
write a report and present in class in the next lesson using a chart or a digital device.
Conclusion: learners are guided to write related verse from the Scripture on a flashcard, recite it, and display it in class.
Reflection: The teacher makes an honest evaluation / contemplate learning points on areas that worked well, worked
less or did not work, This is achieved through asking questions/giving assignments on taught concepts. Assess if
learners can answer or perform the task/assignments if not what are the remedies does the teacher give remedial teaching
or reteach the concept and make it more practical/involve learners.

National Goals of Education
1. Foster nationalism, patriotism and promote national unity
2. Promote social, economic, technological and industrial needs for national
development
3. Promote individual development and self-fulfilment
4. Promote sound moral and religious values
5. Promote social equity and responsibility
6. Promote respect for and development of Kenya’s rich and varied cultures
7. Promote international consciousness and foster positive attitudes towards
other nations
8. Promote positive attitudes towards good health and environmental
protection.
ACHIEVEMENT OF NATIONAL GOALS OF EDUCATION
THROUGH THE COMPETENCY BASED CURRICULUM
❑The Competency Based Curriculum focuses on acquisition of
the desired knowledge, skills, values and attitudes to cope
with contemporary life challenges.
❑Learning outcomes are derived from the National Goals of
Education.
❑The achievement of learning outcomes leads to desired
behavioral change.
LEARNING OUTCOMES
❑Learning outcomes are the end result or what the learner is able to
demonstrate upon completion of a lesson, sub strand, strand or level.
❑Learning outcomes are expressed through the application of
knowledge, skills and attitudes.
❑Learning outcomes express what a learner is expected to do after
going through a learning experience.
❑They indicate the expected observable behavioural changes in the
learner after a learning experience.
Categories of Learning Outcomes in the
Curriculum Design

outcomes.
LEVEL LEARNING OUTCOMES FOR
MIDDLE SCHOOL EDUCATION
By the end of Middle School, the learner should be able to:
1) apply literacy, numeracy skills and logical thinking appropriately in self-expression,
2) communicate effectively in diverse contexts,
3) apply digital literacy skills appropriately for communication and learning in
day-to-day life,
4) practise hygiene, appropriate sanitation and nutrition to promote health,
5) explore, manipulate, manage and conserve the environment effectively for learning
and sustainable development,
6) demonstrate ethical behaviour and exhibit good citizenship as a civic responsibility,
7) demonstrate social skills, spiritual and moral values for peaceful co-existence,
8) demonstrate appreciation of the country’s rich, diverse cultural heritage for
harmonious co-existence,
9) manage Pertinent and Contemporary Issues in society effectively
Activity: Relationship between the learning outcomes
and the National Goals of Education
1.Pick on any National Goal of Education
2.Identify one level learning outcome for middle school that will help realise the
National Goal of Education in N0 1 above.
3.Identify one subject/general learning outcome that will aid realization of the level
learning outcome in N0. 2 above.
4.From any learning area, pick one specific learning outcome that will help achieve the
subject general learning outcome identified in 3 above
5. Wrap up the session by discussing the relationship that exists between the national
goals and various outcomes. Participants should also not that all outcomes are derived
from the national goals.
Progression of Learning outcomes
Essence statements
Statements that describe:
❑ Why a subject is taught at a certain level
❑The strands in the subject
❑Learning approaches to be used
❑Theoretical underpinning for the subject
Specific learning outcomes
Since CBC is learner centred and activity oriented, learning
outcomes are designed following the same trend.
The outcome statement includes a verb that will clearly
illustrate what action learners need to engage in to
demonstrate their competencies.
The action could demonstrate a change at the level of
knowledge, a skill or an attitude.
Example:
By the end of the sub strand the learner should be able to:
a) identify types of soil erosion in the environment (knowledge)
b) control soil erosion in the school environment (skills)
c) appreciate the role of soil conservation in maintaining agricultural environment
(attitude).
The verbs represent the three domains of learning.
A good learning outcome begins with an action verb, followed by the object of the verb
and a phrase that gives the context.
Other verbs that can be use instead of appreciate include acknowledge, advocate,
value, embrace, recognise among others
Characteristics of good specific learning outcomes
a) The specific learning outcomes should be observable.
b) Specific learning outcomes are agreeable to assessment.
c) Avoids vague immeasurable terms like know, understand,
learn etc
Activity
Studying Specific Learning Outcomes in Curriculum
Design
1. Use a sample curriculum design (any learning area)
2. Identify and study specific learning outcomes from several
subjects
3. Discuss the verbs used in creating them
Writing Learning outcomes
Begin each specific learning outcome with an action verb,
followed by the object of the verb followed by a phrase that gives
the context.
Preferably use only one verb per learning outcome.
Avoid vague terms like know, understand, learn, be familiar with,
be exposed to, be acquainted with, and be aware of,
demonstrate understanding.
The specific learning outcomes must be observable.
Ensure that the specific learning outcomes are capable of being
assessed

• Acquisition of facts, ideas, concepts; their application,
KNOWLEDGE        synthesis to get new ideas and evaluation of the information
• Using the knowledge acquired, a learner is able to apply it to
perform certain tasks against a given standard. The standard
SKILLS        to which a learner should perform the task is referred to as a
competence.
• Desirable beliefs and personal attributes that a learner
VALUES         acquires through knowledge and skill that influence
performance.

INTERPRETATION OF JSS SIGN LANGUAGE SKILLS
CURRICULUM DESIGNS
INTRODUCTION
This session guides the participants on how to interpret the
Junior Secondary Sign language skills curriculum designs.
Participants are expected to interrogate the curriculum designs
and interpret the various components for effective
implementation.
INTRODUCTION
• Sign language is a visual and gestural language used for communication as
an alternative to speech. It incorporates hand signs, body language, facial
expressions, lip patterns, and finger spelling.
• Sign language shall be offered to regular learners as one of the optional
learning areas in junior secondary education. This language will rely on
English language structure in signing sentences. The skills in sign language
acquired at this level will form the basis for further language development
and specialisation in the subsequent levels of learning. This will result in a
nation where people from all walks of life can use their sign language skills,
breaking down communication barriers between people with hearing
impairment and people who can hear, and thus improving social interaction
and cohesion
SKILLS IN SIGN LANGUAGE INCLUDE:
 Observing and signing (listening and speaking)
 Sign reading and interpreting (Reading)
 Presenting and writing (Writing)
 Grammar
ESSENCE STATEMENT
• The goal of learning sign language skills is to provide regular
learners with the ability to communicate and socialise with people
who do not speak, particularly those with are Hearing Impairment.
• The introduction of sign language skills to regular learners at this
level gives the learner the opportunity to develop competencies in
expressive and receptive communication, that is, Observing and
signing, Sign reading and interpreting, Writing and presenting.
These skills will be applied to the signed text in its exact English
structure.
GENERAL LEARNING OUTCOMES
• By the end of the junior secondary school the learner should be
able to:
1. Observe signed conversation in diverse contexts and respond
effectively.
2. Use Sign Language to express oneself effectively in conversations.
3. Demonstrate ability to interact appropriately with persons who
are deaf using Sign language.
4. Interpret correctly and fluently within an inclusive educational
setup.
5. Utilize acquired sign language skills to address divergent pertinent
and contemporary issues in the society.

KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS
When writing the key inquiry questions the teacher should utilise the typical question words:
How? Why? Or What or which? Depending on the concept being learned
From the above sub strand the following key inquiry questions have been developed to facilitate
the learning experiences in the two lessons;
• Lesson 1 KIQs
a) Which signs, words or actions show etiquette?
b) How do we identify etiquette in social interactions?
c) Why is etiquette important in social interaction?
• Lesson 2 KIQs
a) How do we demonstrate signing etiquette during conversations?
b) How do we use non manual features to show etiquette when signing?
SUGGESTED LEARNING EXPERIENCES
 In pairs, learners brainstorm words and phrases such as Greetings, thank you, sorry, excuse, please among
others that demonstrate etiquette when signing. The competency of communication and collaboration is
developed as learners form groups, choose leaders and share ideas on words and phrases that demonstrate
etiquette.
 Learners watch and analyse a signed video clip on words, phrases and non manual features that
demonstrates etiquette in signing. Social justice is developed as learners correct peers on choice of words
that demonstrate etiquette in conversations.
 In pair, learners sign words and phrases as shown in the video clip. The competency of self efficacy is
developed as learners confidently present and critique peers work.
 Learners observe and sign words and phrases related to signing etiquette displayed on flashcards. The
competency of learning to learn is developed as learners acquire signs of different words showing etiquette.
 In pairs, learners construct and sign simple sentences using words, phrases and non manual features that
show etiquette. Creativity and Imagination is enhanced as learners construct simple sentences and sign
them while supporting with non manual features to show etiquette in signing. Life skills is nurtured as
learners take turns and use appropriate non manual features to show etiquette.
LEARNING APROACHES
To facilitate this sub strand, the following learning steps and facilitation strategies could be used:
• Inquiry based learning.
IBL involves providing experiences that enable learners to develop understanding about aspects of the world
around them through the development and use of investigative skills. IBL incorporate a process of exploring
the world, which leads to: asking questions, making discoveries (KIQ) and conducting research and
experiments.
• Experiential learning
When using Experiential learning process, the learner is actively engaged in posing questions, investigating,
experimenting, being curious, solving problems, assuming responsibility, being creative and constructing
meaning using authentic tasks.
• Task analysis
This involves breaking down the concept or skill into smaller teachable steps to allow all learners to
participate and support each other in the learning process.
• Demonstration
The teacher demonstrates what the learners are to carry out. The teacher, a resource person, or another
learner can try out a target activity involving signing etiquette for other learners to see, watch, observe,
and imitate.
LEARNING RESOURCES
Learning resources that can be used to facilitate this sub strand include:
●    Digital devices (to capture and record demonstrations when signing etiquette skills)
●    KSL/SL dictionary to get signs of words
●    Text books reference on hints to fluent signing
●    Flash cards- displaying words and phrases related to signing etiquette
●    Mirror to view facial expressions for self assessment
In this sub strand the following modes of assessment can be used:
●    Observation
●    Oral or signed questions
●    Written assessment

PERTINENT AND
CONTEMPORARY
ISSUES (PCIs)
A Presentation by:
KICD
Date: 02/12/2020
Page 1 of 11
Introducing PCIs
• What are PCIs?
• Open Discussions!!!!
• Pertinent - having a clear decisive relevance to the
matter at hand
• Contemporary - marked by characteristics of the
present period; thus being, MORDEN, CURRENT
Page 2 of 11
PCIs Explained
• Children are faced with a myriad of
challenges and issues owing to the
social-cultural and economic dynamics
in the society.
• The Competence-Based-Curriculum
calls them Pertinent and Contemporary
Issues
• Previously being referred to as
emerging issues and/or Cross-cutting
issues.
Page 3 of 11
Cont’d
• Learner-centered education goes
beyond the subject content.
• It instills appropriate
competencies the learner requires
in order to effectively address the
PCIs of everyday life; thereby
leading a fulfilled life as well as
becoming a productive member of
the society
Page 4 of 11
Examples of PCIs
• Citizenship education – includes Peace
education, Integrity, Ethnic and racial
relations, social cohesion, Patriotism and
good governance, child’s rights, child care
and protection
• Health education – includes HIV and
AIDS, Alcohol and Substance use, Life style
diseases, personal hygiene, Communicable
and chronic diseases e.g. COVID-19
• Life Skills & Human sexuality – includes
Life skills education and human sexuality
Page 5 of 11
Examples of PCIs- Cont’d
• Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) –
includes Environmental Education, DRR, Safety
and security Education (small arms, human
trafficking, Poverty eradication, Countering
terrorism, radicalization,) Gender and Animal
Welfare Education.
Page 6 of 11
Mainstreaming PCIs
• PCIs have been mainstreamed in the three
dimensions of the curriculum, that is:
• The Formal;
• The Non-Formal; and
• The In-formal.
Note: The mainstreaming of PCIs has to be
deliberate and based on a conscious effort.
PCIs become apart of the content being
delivered
Page 7 of 11
Formal Dimension
• A relevant and suitable sub strand or sub
theme in a learning area/subject is identified
where PCIs can appropriately be incorporated
and taught alongside the subject matter .
Example:
Learning area: Social Studies (Grade 4)
Strand: Natural and Built Environment
Sub strand: Physical features in the County
Learning Outcome: (c) adopt responsible behaviour to
conserve the physical features.
PCIs: Promotion of environmental conservation as
learners appreciate the natural and built environment
in the County.
Page 8 of 11
Non-formal
• These are organized, structured and systematic
learning activities (NFPs) that take place in
school. They support acquisition of knowledge,
values and skills learnt in class.
Page 9 of 11
Informal
• This refers to the Knowledge, Attitudes and
Skills or behaviour acquired by learners from
the social interaction with members of the
school community. Exemplary behaviours and
appropriate values can easily be emulated.
Page 10 of 11
At the end…….
• PCIs make learning relevant
• Our commitments to Lesson delivery

JUNIOR SECONDARY LEVEL
PERTINENT AND CONTEMPORARY ISSUES
(PCIs)
Session Objectives
By the end of the session, the participant should be able to:
a) Explain the meaning of Pertinent and Contemporary Issues
(PCIs) in Society;
b) Examine the nature of Pertinent and Contemporary Issues (PCIs)
in society;
c) Describe the process of mainstreaming Pertinent and
Contemporary Issues (PCIs) in the day-to-day learning; and
d) Appreciate the importance of mainstreaming Pertinent and
Contemporary Issues (PCIs) in the day-to-day learning
KWL
• 1. What I know about ….........
• 2. What I want to know about
…............
INTRODUCTION
• Mainstreaming of Pertinent and Contemporary Issues (PCIs) is one of the
major initiatives in ongoing curriculum reform process.
• Learners are faced with a myriad of challenges and issues owing to the
social-cultural and economic dynamics in the society.
• These issues are referred to as Pertinent and Contemporary
Issues(PCIs) in education because of the impact they can have on the
learner and learning.
• They have the potential to affect learner’s psychosocial wellbeing, access
to education, retention, transition, completion and ultimately
advancement in the world of work.
• Can we identify the challenges that learners are facing in their daily
lives???
THE PLACE OF PCIs IN THE BECF
• During the National survey that was conducted in 2016 to
inform development of Competency Based Curriculum, a
number of issues were identified and found pertinent for
inclusion in the curriculum.
• Findings from other Educational researches and best
practices in other countries also informed identification of
PCIs to be mainstreamed in the curriculum
IDENTIFICATION OF PCIs FOR MAINSTREAMING
• The Basic Education Curriculum Framework (BECF), outlines
these issues under various categories of Pertinent and
Contemporary Issues (PCIs)
• The framework also provides guidance on how PCIs should be
mainstreamed through the formal, non-formal and the informal
dimensions of the curriculum.
CATEGORIES OF PCIs
In Junior School, the following categories of PCIs have been
mainstreamed in the curriculum:
 Health Promotion Issues (HPIs)
 Life Skills Education and Human Sexuality
 Education for Sustainable Development/Socio-Economic and
Environmental Issues
 Learner Support Programmes (LSPs)
 Parental Empowerment and Engagement (PE&E)
 Citizenship Issues in Education/Citizenship Education

MAINSTREAMING PROCESS OF PCIs
Formal Dimension
A relevant and suitable sub strand or sub theme in a learning
area/subject is identified where PCIs can appropriately be
incorporated and taught alongside the subject matter .
Example: Learning area: Social Studies (Grade 7)
Strand: People and Population
Sub strand: Human Diversity and Inclusion
Learning Experience: Debate on ways of applying inclusion in their
day-to-day interactions
PCI: Promotion of social cohesion as learners debate on ways of
applying inclusion in day to day interactions.
Cont…MAINSTREAMING PROCESS
Formal Dimension
In every sub strand in the design , there is a component referred to as ‘link to
PCIs’. This is where PCIs to be mainstreamed in the sub strand are indicated in
the curriculum designs
Example: Social Studies grade 7:
Pertinent and Contemporary Issues (PCIs):
 Social cohesion as learners’ research in groups on factors
influencing population distribution in Africa.
 Self-esteem as learners do presentations in class on factors
influencing population distribution in Africa.
 Online safety as learners use digital resources to establish
settlement patterns
Cont…MAINSTREAMING PROCESS
Non-formal Dimension
• These are organised, structured and systematic learning activities
(NFPs) that take place in school or out of school. They support
acquisition of knowledge, values and skills learnt in class.
• All the PCIs mainstreamed in the formal dimension of the
curriculum, can also be mainstreamed in NFPs such as games,
sports, clubs and societies among others.
Cont…MAINSTREAMING PROCESS
Informal Dimension
It’s also referred to as the hidden curriculum. It refers to the
Knowledge, Attitudes and Skills or behaviour acquired by learners
from the social interaction with members of the school community,
parents among others.
There is no organized learning programme in this dimension.
Learners develop competencies as they interact with other people.
That is why, a conducive environment should be cultivated for
learners to acquire appropriate behaviours and nurture values.
CONCLUSION
Effective mainstreaming of PCIs calls for deliberate effort from
teachers to ensure these issues are addressed during the learning
experiences
Creativity is also required to ensure that the PCIs are well
mainstreamed
There is need to be keen on contextual issues since various issues
are different in various circumstances .
Mainstreaming of PCIs will enable the learners to develop
appropriate competencies in order to address the challenges they
grapple with in their daily lives, thereby leading fulfilled lives as well
as becoming productive members of the society.

Constitution of Kenya, 2010

for the world of work, career progression and sustainable development.

innovation and creativity and ICT .

Ways Of Reinforcing Cognitive Development

Academic engagement
• Provide learning experiences that cater to their interest.
• Avoid negative labels such as “failure”. Focus on helping them progress
towards achievement of learning outcomes by providing constructive feedback
on tasks.
• Provide opportunities for learners to showcase competencies learnt and
compliment efforts. This enables them acquire self efficacy.
Reinforcing cognitive development cont’d
Build on already acquired knowledge, skills and values
• The learners will fall back on what they have learnt in previous grades as a
basis for understanding new content presented to them.
• Teachers should therefore link related knowledge and skills progressively
moving from known to unknown.
• Transfer of learning and reinforcement of learnt concepts will enhance
learning new knowledge and skills.
Reinforcing cognitive development cont’d
Provide Practical Learning Experiences
Engage learners in authentic learning experiences that connect to the world
around them. Provide experiential learning characterized by
•   Learner-centered pedagogy,
• peer and self-assessment
•   practical activities will be effective in promoting learning. A pragmatic
approach to instruction will enhance the achievement of learning outcomes.
Reinforcing cognitive development cont’d
Adopt instructional approaches that enable learners develop
competencies
▪ Involve the learner in discussions, experimentations, research and
debates over curricula, social, moral and global issues. This will
allow them to think critically.
▪ Provide learning experiences that allow for manipulation of
various ICT devices. Integration of ICT in learning will cater to the
interest of the learner thus making learning enjoyable.
Reinforcing cognitive development cont’d
Involve learners in decision making
• Learners can tell their strengths and weaknesses. Furthermore, they often
self-advocate. They are now able to identify areas they are good in and take
up tasks that they can competently execute.
• Learners should therefore be guided to set realistic goals for the future. Their
input is crucial in identifying skills and talents.

Session Objectives
To give an overview of Grade 7 French curriculum designs.
To demonstrate the transformative methodologies to be used in
learning French in Grade 7.
To interpret Grade 7 French curriculum designs.
INTRODUCTION
• French language is one of the foreign languages taught in Kenyan schools. In
the competency-based curriculum, the French language is taught from grade
4. At grade 7, learners cover the four skills, listening and speaking, reading
and writing. These four skills are further broken down to sub skills. In Strand
three, the writing skill is broken down into; guided writing, descriptive
writing, creative writing and functional creative writing.
Essence statement:
French at Junior secondary builds on the linguistic competencies acquired in
upper primary. The proposed learning experiences provide the opportunity
to experiment with and explore the language in contextualized
communication situations. The content is delivered using interactive and
participatory methods of learning aimed at unlocking the learners ‘multiple
intelligences.
STRANDS
1.Listening and speaking
2.Reading
3.Writing
4.Language structures

• Listening and   • Social interaction
speaking        • Immediate Family
• Reading         • Our room
• Writing         • Media
• Language        • School
structures      • Shopping
• Hobbies
• Health
Unique Area
Intercultural approach
• Learning French as a foreign language calls for an appreciation of the French culture on which the language
itself is anchored. In this case, the Intercultural learning approach involves exposing the learners to various
aspects of the way of life in the francophone world before requiring them to compare these with what goes
on in their own cultures.
• Learners are exposed to virtual visits to sites of interest in the francophone world to enrich their
experiences.
• Learners could use language learning applications on the internet and create communities of learning to
develop their intercultural awareness skills. Such practice will help in developing positive attitude and a
good measure of tolerance of other cultures. These approach enables the learners to observe, to compare,
and to contrast their culture and the French culture, thereby raising their awareness and understanding
these will make them accept and appreciate cultural differences. For instance, in sub strand 1.7Listening
Comprehension and Oral expression: Hobbies, you could engage the learners in learning activities where
they compare hobby activities in Kenya and France.
Approche actionnelle
• In this approach, the learner is considered a social actor
in the learning process- an active participant who engages
in tasks in a cultural contextor real life experience.
• The learner is given a realistic scenario with a problem to
solve. an inclusive and social environment is cultivated to
promote cooperation.
• Discussion in pairs or groups are encouraged to create a
sense of belonging in the community.

1. Practice typing skills using MS Word/Office and French shortcut keys

with different accent marks (accent aigu, accent gravex accent circonflexe…)

shortcut keys.

on the class notice board

keyboard steps on safe handling of media devices.
•        (ii) The learner could write down the steps of safely switching on and
off media devices.
• They could then share their work with others by posting the write-ups on
the notice board of the classroom.

CBC TRAINING OF GRADE 7 TEACHERS
INDIGENOUS LANGAUGES
MARCH 2023
Introduction
• Indigenous Languages is an optional subject in Grade 7 and has been
allocated 3 lessons per week. The Indigenous languages design is
organised into strands and sub strands. The strands are as follows:
Listening and speaking, Reading, Language structure and
Writing.
• For each of the strands, a theme has been provided to a context for
language learning. Learners will be expected to conduct all the
activities in the Indigenous Language. The learning area will best be
handled by a teacher who is proficient in the Indigenous language
and has acquired the pedagogical content knowledge in the languages
Rationale for Indigenous Languages
• Learners in Junior Secondary School will be exposed to Indigenous
Languages because a people’s culture is best passed on through their
language. In addition, mother tongue, like any other language, is
central to the success or failure of education and development
programmes.
• The need for Indigenous languages is articulated in the Constitution
in Chapter 2, Article 7 (3).
• Goal of education N0. 6 Promote respect for and development of
Kenya’s rich and varied cultures
• A reasonable proficiency in mother tongue at this level will be a
prerequisite for a mother tongue course at senior secondary.
STRANDS AND SUB STRANDS
Listening and   Listening for information and for pleasure, listening for
speaking        comprehension, attentive listening, conversational skills,
intensive Listening, storytelling, presentation skills
Reading         Reading for information, reading for pleasure, reading for
comprehension, extensive reading, library skills, intensive
reading

structure       sentences

information, imaginative and Creative Writing, narrative
writing

Unpacking a sample skill
Strand: 3.3 Language Structure
Sub strand: 3.3.1 Word classes
Skill: 1. identify verbs used in passages on safety and security; use verbs to construct
sentences
Suggested real life experiences (non-formal activities) that can be used to facilitate
acquisition of the skill, competencies and values
Engaging peers in a language game during clubs and societies in which they identify
verbs from texts. They can then construct messages on safety and security using the
verbs learnt, then post them in strategic places in the school. This enhances creativity
and imagination as well as patriotism.
Unpacking a sample skill
• Suggested transformative pedagogy:
i) Collaborative and Problem based leaning – Learning verbs in
contexts such as passages, poems, songs, riddles, tongue twisters and
stories.
Learners can be given a passage then asked to read it and underline all
the verbs on the theme of safety and security. They should then construct
sentences which will be peer reviewed by other learners.
Passage
Ūsūvīo na ūseseei nī wa vata mūnene maūndūnī maītu ma kīla
müthenya. Kīla ūmwe waītū nīwaīle kūīkīīthya kana twī ngūnūū yīūlū
wa kīla kīendeeye maūthyūlūkonī maītu.
Yīla twoona andū twīna makana namo, nī twaīlītwe nī uvīkya ūvoo kwa
aseseeī ma mūūo mītukī.
Tūīmīnūkīlya, nītwaīle kūmanya atūi maītū nesa. Kwa ngelekanyo,
mawīa ala makūnaa, makwate kyaūya Kya kīla müthenya na kūmanya
ala makwatīanīaa namo. Kwa kwīka ou, tūikethaa tūīsūvīa mūuo wītū
w'oka, īndī vamwe na atūi maītū.
Translation
Translation
Safety and security is very important in our day-to-day-
lives. Each one of us needs to ensure that we are alert of
what is going on in our environment. When we see
suspicious people, we should report them to the security
officers immediately. Lastly, we should know our
neighbours well. For example, what they do for a living
and who they relate with. By doing so, we will not only
be protecting ourselves but our neighbours too.
ii) Collaborative learning and problem based learning – Cross word
puzzle
Learners can be asked to search for the verbs and verb phrases from a
cross word puzzle in pairs: downwards, upwards, backwards, across,
horizontally and diagonally.
Note
This puzzle was prepared for the Kikamba language in mind and with
reference to the activity on the passage above.

• major curriculum reform to align it with the

• reforming the education sector to provide for the
holistic development of learners

• introduction of values

Summative evaluation of the 8-4-4 system of education, 2009
• more academic and examination oriented. Teachers hardly use
formative assessment (assessment for learning). Assessment was
limited to summative assessment (assessment of learning).
• graduates at secondary school level also did not acquire adequate
entrepreneurial skills for self-reliance.
• did not provide flexible education pathways for identifying and
nurturing aptitudes, talents and interests of learners early enough in
order to prepare them for the world of work, career progression and
sustainable development.
• skills gaps identified - agricultural, entrepreneurial, vocational and
technical skills, innovation and creativity and ICT .
• recommended a needs assessment survey

KICD Needs Assessment Survey 2016
• a curriculum reform
• a wide curriculum to cater for various talent areas to
enable learners achieve their potential and be better
equipped to develop themselves and the nation.
• a functional holistic curriculum that would produce an
individual with spiritual, moral and social aspects with
ability to live amicably with others.
• development and acquisition competencies at every
level of learning
• a flexible and comprehensive educational structure and
system

1.0 INTRODUCTION
The Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) has developed curriculum designs
for Grade 7, 8 and 9 for learners following age based pathway and Prevocational Level for
learners following stage based pathway. To ensure effective delivery of the curriculum, the
Institute in collaboration with the Teachers Service Commission (TSC) has organised
elaborate training programmes for teachers in Junior School and Prevocational Level.
KICD has developed this Facilitators Training Manual to enable training of curriculum
implementers for efficient curriculum implementation in Grade 7, 8 and 9 and Prevocational
Level. The training manual focuses on the pedagogical approaches of facilitating learning to
different categories of learners with special needs. Further, the manual guides participants on
how to adapt resources and assessment methods in the various subjects/learning areas in
junior school and pre vocational level.
Aims of the Training
The aims of the training are to:
a) equip participants with the necessary knowledge, skills and attitudes to effectively
implement the Competency Based Curriculum;
b) equip participants with skills to facilitate differentiated inclusive learning to ensure
that all learners are fully engaged in the learning process.
Structure of the Manual
In each session, the manual outlines the following:
•   Session outcomes.
•   Session activity.
•   Facilitators notes.
•   Reflections.
iii
SESSION 1: INTRODUCTION
This session addresses the overview of Junior school for learners with visual, hearing,
physical impairment as well as learners in pre vocational level of the stage based pathway.
Note : Graduate from primary school joins junior school at grade 7.
By the end of the session, the participant should be able to
a) describe characteristics of learners in junior school and pre-vocational level.
b) examine learner centres pedagogies for junior school and pre vocational level
In groups, participants
a) brainstorm on the overview of junior school and pre-vocational level and do a plenary
presentation
b) discuss on the characteristics of learners in junior school and at pre vocational level
c) search the learner centred pedagogies for junior school and pre vocational level.
Facilitator’s notes
Learners join the junior school after completing upper primary. Junior School exposes learners
to a broad based curriculum to enable them to explore their own abilities, personality and
potential as a basis for choosing subjects according to career paths of interest at the senior
school. Learners in junior school are exposed to all learning areas to enable them make
informed choices as they transition to senior school. Learners learn in junior school for a
duration of three years.

LEARNER CENTRED PEDAGOGIES FOR JUNIOR SCHOOL
Pedagogy refers to sets of learning experiences that facilitate achievement of specified learning
outcomes. Learner centered pedagogical approaches include:
Inquiry Based learning:
•   Learners construct knowledge and meaning from their own experiences.
•   Learners are engaged in, questioning, reasoning and experiential (hands-on activities).
Problem-based learning (PBL)
•   Learners are involved in solving authentic, open-ended, structured, real-world problems.
•   Learners are engaged in extended processes of asking questions, finding resources and
applying learnt information.
Play Based Learning
•   Employs plays as the primary means for learners to explore the world, investigate its properties
and build an understanding of how it works.
•   Play fosters curiosity, creativity, and problem-solving skills. It supports learners’ well-being,
resilience, motivation and engagement & prepares learners for life- long learning.
Project Based Learning
•  Learners gain knowledge and skills by working for an extended period of time to investigate
and respond to authentic, engaging and complex tasks, questions, problems or challenges.
• Learners drive their own learning through inquiry, as they work collaboratively to research and
create projects that reflect their innate potential and talents.
Blended Learning
Involves integrating traditional face-to-face instruction with technology.
Cooperative learning
Involves learners working in small groups collaboratively to accomplish assigned tasks.
Design-based learning (DBL)
Entails the use of open ended, hands-on and challenging experiences that allow learners to apply
theoretical knowledge to develop new ways of solving real-life problems.
Experiential learning
This is learning through reflection, where Learning Experiences are structured and learners take
initiative, make decisions and are accountable for the results. Examples include field trips and
excursions.
OVERVIEW OF PREVOCATIONAL LEVEL
PREVOCATIONAL LEVEL CURRICULUM
The specialised curriculum at the prevocational level, which is predominantly skill- based,
prepares learners with disabilities for basic work skills. At this level, learners are introduced to the
pre-requisite skills in various vocational skill areas to enable them to identify their abilities and
interests in a given field.
The Prevocational Level curriculum designs have been developed for the following categories of
learners with special needs; learners with Intellectual Disability, Deafblindness, Severe Autism,
Severe Cerebral Palsy and Multiple Disabilities.
Categories of Learners at Prevocational Level
Learners with Intellectual disabilities
These are learners with significant subaverage general intellectual functioning existing concurrently
with deficits in adaptive behaviour and manifested during the developmental period that adversely
affects the learner’s educational performance. Learners with intellectual disabilities are classified
into four major categories. These are learners with:
• Mild Intellectual Disabilities
• Moderate Intellectual Disabilities
• Severe Intellectual Disabilities
• Profound Intellectual Disabilities
Characteristics of learners with intellectual disabilities
● Slowness in learning due to delayed rate of intellectual development.
● Being unnecessarily slow in carrying out tasks.
● Learning and memory capabilities are significantly below average in comparison to peers
without disabilities.
● Are deficient in relating information to new situations
● Not able to understand what is said or follow instructions.
● Having trouble focusing on relevant stimuli in learning and in real life situations.
● Having difficulty in both learning and applying skills for a number of reasons, including a
higher level of distractibility, inattentiveness, failure to read social cues, and impulsive
behaviour.
● Having delayed speech, language comprehension and formulation difficulties.
● Failing to develop social and emotional relationships
● Having retarded motor development.
● Lacking rhythm in movement
● Having difficulties in remembering experiences or things learnt.
● Lacking motivation.
● Excessive drooling
● Having excessive purposeless movements
● Having difficulty in paying attention or focusing on an activity to its completion.
● Having difficulty in seeing the consequences of their actions.
● Have slow cognitive processing time.
● Have limited self-care skills and independent living skills
Learners with Deafblindness
These are learners with concomitant visual and hearing impairments, the combination of which
causes such severe communication and other developmental and education needs.
Categories of Learners who are deafblind
Learners with deafblindness are of four categories:
•   Congenitally deafblind.
•   Congenitally deaf with acquired blindness
•   Congenitally blind with acquired deafness.
•   Adventitiously deafblind (Aquired Deafness and Aquired Blindness).
General Characteristics of learners who are deafblind
●    Difficulty communicating or an inability to communicate in a meaningful way.
●    Have a distorted perception of the world.
●    Have difficulty in establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships information from
the surrounding.
●    Have medical problems that lead to serious developmental delays.
●    Presence of a combined vision and hearing losses
●   Tactile sensitivity and resistance to being touched.
●   Delays in motor development.
●   Difficulty following a conversation
●   Appear to be withdrawn and isolated
●   May be deprived of many of the most basic extrinsic motivations
●   Self-stimulatory behaviours resulting from sensory deprivation, isolation, frustration,
confusion and fear.
●   Have unique learning styles.
●   Difficulty in generalizing information learned to other settings.
●   Feeding difficulties and or unusual sleeping patterns.
●   May have difficulty anticipating what is going to happen. Clues from the environment or from
the faces/actions of others may be difficult to read.
●   Difficulty navigating the environment
Learners with Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs)
Autism spectrum disorders are neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by an impairment in
social reciprocity, atypical communication, and repetitive behaviours. Learners with ASDs often
have difficulties with social communication and interaction, and restricted or repetitive behaviors
or interests. Further, they may also have different ways of learning, moving, or paying attention.
Characteristics of learners with Autism spectrum disorders
● Lines up toys or other objects and gets upset when order is changed.
● Repeats words or phrases over and over (echolalia).
● Plays with toys the same way every time.
● Is focused on parts of objects (for example, wheels).
● Gets upset by minor changes.
● Has obsessive interests.
● Tendency toward following certain routines routine.
● Difficult time with social interactions.
● Stereotyped movements such as flaps hands, rocks body, or runs/spins self in circles, flipping
light switches, hand waving, toe walking.
● Has unusual reactions to the way things sound, smell, taste, look, or feel.
● Delayed language skills.
● Delayed movement skills.
● Delayed cognitive or learning skills.
● Hyperactive, impulsive, and/or inattentive behaviour.
● Has epilepsy or seizure disorder.
● Unusual eating and sleeping habits.
● Gastrointestinal issues (for example, constipation)
● Unusual mood or emotional reactions.
10
● Anxiety, stress, or excessive worry.
● Lack of fear or more fear than expected.
Learners with Severe Cerebral palsy (CP)
Cerebral palsy is a disorder of movement and posture that is caused by a nonprogressive
abnormality of the immature brain that affect the learner’s ability to move and maintain balance
and posture. Learners with Cerebral Palsy are classified into four major categories. These are
learners with;
•   increased muscle tone/ stiff muscles (Spastic Cerebral Palsy)
•   abnormalities in muscle tone that involve the whole body/ uncontrollable movements
(Dyskinetic Cerebral Palsy.)
•   abnormalities of voluntary movement involving balance and position of the trunk and
limbs in space/ poor balance and coordination (Ataxic Cerebral Palsy.)
•   more than one type of cerebral palsy/ more than one type of motor pattern is present
(Mixed Cerebral Palsy.)
General characteristics of learners with severe cerebral palsy
● Stiff muscles and exaggerated reflexes (spasticity)
● Variations in muscle tone, such as being either too stiff or too floppy
● Stiff muscles with normal reflexes (rigidity)
Lack of balance and muscle coordination (ataxia)
● Tremors or jerky involuntary movement
● Slow, writhing movements
● Difficulty walking
● Difficulty with fine motor skills
● Difficulty speaking
● Excessive drooling or problems with swallowing
● Intellectual disabilities
● Delayed growth, resulting in smaller size than would be expected
● Presence of Seizures (epilepsy)
● Difficulty hearing (deafness)
● Problems with vision and abnormal eye movements
● Abnormal touch or pain sensations
● Bladder and bowel problems, including constipation and urinary incontinence
Learners with Multiple disabilities.
These are learners who have a combination of disabilities. For example, some learners have a
sensory disability with autism, intellectual and/or physical disabilities.
11
General characteristics of learners with multiple disabilities
●     Appear to be withdrawn and isolated
●     Have difficulty in establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships
●     Have limited self-care skills and independent living skills
●     Have medical problems that leads to serious developmental delays.
●     Are defensive of being touched.
●     Have feeding difficulties and or unusual sleeping patterns.
●     May display an immature behavior inconsistent with chronological age.
●     May exhibit an impulsive behavior and low frustration level.
●     May execute self-injurious behavior.
●     Limited speech or communication.
●     Difficulty in basic physical mobility.
●     Trouble generalizing skills from one situation to another.
●     Need for support in major life activities.

LEARNER CENTRED PEDAGOGIES FOR PREVOCATIONAL LEVEL
Pedagogy refers to sets of learning experiences that facilitate achievement of specific learning
outcomes. Some of the learner centred pedagogical approaches for Prevocational level include:
a)    Task Analysis
● Involves breaking down of concepts into smaller, manageable steps to make learning
more achievable.
b)    Diagnostic Prescriptive Instruction approach
● Emphasises assessing (diagnosing) the learners' individual learning needs and
providing adapted instruction (prescribing) to address those specific needs.
● This approach is highly learner-centred and focuses on understanding learners'
strengths and weaknesses to create targeted interventions for improvement.
c)    Multisensory Approach
12
● This involves incorporating visual, auditory, tactile and kinesthetic elements into the
instruction during learning. It also employs use of gestures, facial expressions, and
tactile cues to convey meaning and pairing spoken language with corresponding signs
or tactile representations to reinforce comprehension.
d)   Differentiated learning
● This is an instructional approach that tailors learning strategies, content, and
assessments to accommodate the diverse needs, skills, interests, and learning styles of
learners. Its goal is to ensure that all learners, regardless of their abilities or
backgrounds, have access to the same educational opportunities and can achieve their
highest potential. Differentiation can be applied in various areas of instruction,
including content, process, product, and learning environment.
e)   Modelling
● Modelling is a teaching strategy where the teacher demonstrates a task, skill, or concept
for the learners to observe and imitate. It involves the teacher showing how to perform
a task or solve a problem step-by-step while providing clear, direct examples of the
desired behaviors, tasks, or learning outcomes for learners to observe and imitate.
f)   Tactile Communication and feedback
● Involves using tactile Sign Language, hand-under- hand guidance, or tactile cues
depending on the individual needs of the learner.
● Learners are provided with meaningful touch cues to convey information and reinforce
learning.
g)   Routines
● Involves creating a structured, predictable sequences of activities or behaviours that are
consistently followed in the learning environment and communicating changes on time.
● Routines are integral to creating a structured and safe classroom atmosphere and helps
learners to anticipate what comes next and engage more fully.
● Routines provide stability and a sense of security, which can significantly reduce
anxiety and improve focus.
h)   Repetition
● This refers to the practice of repeatedly presenting information, instructions, tasks, or
activities to help learners gain mastery over them. It provides learners with additional
opportunities to practice and reinforce concepts until they are understood and can be
performed independently.
i) Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS)
● This is an augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) approach used to
support learners with communication difficulties, particularly those with autism
spectrum disorder (ASD) and other developmental disabilities. PECS utilises pictures
or symbols to help students express their wants, needs, and ideas when verbal
communication is limited or absent. PECS empowers learners to communicate more
effectively, increasing their social interaction, independence, and overall quality of life.
j)   Inquiry Based Learning
● Learners construct knowledge and meaning from their own experiences.
13
● Learners are engaged in questioning, reasoning and experiential (hands-on activities)
k)   Problem-Based Learning (PBL)
● Learners are involved in solving authentic, open-ended, structured, real-world
problems.
● Learners are engaged in extended processes of asking questions, finding resources and
applying learnt information.
l)   Play Based Learning
● Employs play as the primary means for learners to explore the world, investigate its
properties and build an understanding of how it works.
● Play fosters curiosity, creativity, and problem-solving skills. It supports learners’ well-
being, resilience, motivation and engagement and prepares learners for life-long
learning.
● Play improves coordination, motor and social skills.
m) Project Based Learning
● Learners gain knowledge and skills by working for an extended period of time to
investigate and respond to authentic, engaging and complex tasks, questions, problems
or challenges.
● Learners drive their own learning through inquiry, as they work collaboratively to
research and create projects that reflect their innate potential and talents.
n)   Blended Learning
● Involves integrating traditional face-to-face instruction with technology.
● Encourages incorporating use of assistive technology tools and software that can
support the different categories learners in their learning
o)   Design-Based Learning (DBL)
● Entails the use of open-ended, hands-on and challenging experiences that allow
learners to apply theoretical knowledge to develop new ways of solving real-life
problems.
● It encourages active learning through pursuing individual learner’s interests, providing
a real-world context to learning, while providing intrinsic motivation.
p)   Cooperative learning
● Involves learners working in small groups collaboratively to accomplish assigned tasks.
q)   Experiential Learning
● This is learning through active engagement with materials. Experiential learning helps
learners to gain practical skills, develop critical thinking skills, problem-solving
abilities and positive attitudes and help to enhance their communication and
collaboration skills. This type of learning can take many forms, including hands-on
activities, simulations, group projects, field trips, apprenticeships that allow learners to
apply theoretical knowledge to real-world experiences.

SESSION 2: INTERPRETATION OF CURRICULUM DESIGNS
Introduction
This session guides participants to identify and interpret the components of the curriculum design
for effective implementation of CBC.
By the end of the session, the participant should be able to:
a) Identify the components of the curriculum designs for effective implementation.
b) Interpret the curriculum designs for effective implementation of learning.
a) Participants peruse through extracts of curriculum designs to identify the components of
curriculum designs.
b) Participants discuss the various components of curriculum designs with emphasis on how
they are interrelated and developed and make presentations in plenary.
Facilitators Notes
Components and interpretation of the curriculum design
The following are the components of a curriculum design and how they are interpreted in CBC.
● National Goals of Education
● Level learning outcomes
● Essence statement
● Subject general learning outcomes
● Strands and sub strands
● Specific learning outcomes
● Suggested learning experiences
● Suggested Key Inquiry Question(s)
● Core competences
● Pertinent and Contemporary Issues
● Values
● Link to other subjects
● Suggested Non-formal activity to support learning
● Suggested learning resources
● Suggested assessment methods
● Suggested assessment rubric
● Community Service Learning
15
National goals of education
These are the goals that the country has set to achieve through provision of accessible, quality and
relevant education. Kenya has eight national goals that should be achieved through education.
Level learning outcomes
These are demonstrable attributes that are expected in a learner after completing a given level of
education, for example middle school education or Prevocational level.
Essence Statement
An essence statement gives a general overview of a subject. It summarises the fundamental ideas of
each subject. It also explains the rationale and justification of inclusion of the subjects in the
curriculum
Strand and Sub Strand
● A strand is a broad area of study within a specific subject. It is a consistent phenomenological
idea or concept that runs through the subject.
● A strand also cuts across all levels of education.
● A sub-strand represents smaller concepts within the strand.
Learning outcomes
They are the end result of what the learner is able to demonstrate upon completion of a lesson, sub-
strand, strand, subject or level.
Categories of learning outcomes
i)   Level learning outcomes
These are the demonstrable end results expected in learners after having gone through a specific
level of CBC education. For example, Early Years, Middle School Education and Senior School
Education. They are stated in general terms.
ii) General learning outcomes
These learning outcomes indicate what the learner is expected to achieve in a given subject
iii) Specific Learning Outcomes
Specific learning outcomes indicate the expected observable changes in the learner after covering
a sub-strand or a lesson. They specify what the learner should know, is able to do and
demonstrate after participating and completing a given sub-strand or lesson.
• Outcomes are usually expressed through the application of knowledge, skills and attitudes.
Specific learning outcome should have the following components:
• The action verb (the verb represents the three domains of learning including knowledge,
skills and attitudes).
• The object of the verb (the outcome should also have an object, which answers the question
“what”).
• The context (the outcome also has a context, which answers the questions “why”, “where”,
‘’how” and “when”).
16
Suggested learning experiences
Learning experiences comprise of activities that the learner is engaged in during the lesson. The
activities may be carried out by an individual learner or as a group work activity. However, they
should ultimately enable the learner to achieve the intended specific learning outcomes of the lesson.
Learning experiences enable the learner to:
• Acquire knowledge, skills and develop attitudes
• Acquire the intended competences
• Acquire values, pertinent and contemporary issues
• Learn from one another
• Self-regulate and evaluate
• Engage deeply in the subject matter
• Reflect on the learning process
• Interact with others during the learning process
Key Inquiry Question(s)
Key Inquiry Question(s) (KIQ) is an approach where the teacher uses questions to prod learners
thinking to allow them to create information using their own words and understanding. They;
• help to focus the learning,
• probe for deeper meaning and set the stage for further questioning,
• foster the development of critical thinking skills and higher order capabilities such as
problem solving,
• allow learners to explore ideas in an open-ended, non-judgmental, meaningful and
purposeful way,
• encourage collaboration amongst learners, teachers, and the community and integrate
technology to support the learning process.
Writing Key Inquiry Question(s)
Consider the focus of your learning outcome and the sub strands as given in the curriculum design
Core Competencies to be developed
A competency is the ability to apply appropriate knowledge, skills, attitudes and values to
successfully perform a task. Core Competencies are sets of intellectual, personal, social and
emotional proficiencies that students should develop in order to engage in deep, lifelong
learning. The core competencies are developed through exposing the learner to stimulating
learning experiences. The learning areas serve as vehicles through which the core competencies
are developed over time.
The seven core competencies to be developed are:
• Communication and collaboration
• Critical thinking and problem solving
• Imagination and creativity
• Digital literacy
• Citizenship
• Learning to learn and
• Self-efficacy.
17
VALUES
These are principles, qualities , beliefs or standards that guide an individual to respond or
behave in a given circumstance or situation.Values influence how we feel, act and make
choices in life. Nurturing of values will facilitate the achievement of moulding ethical citizens.
Values are intended to address the prevailing societal challenges and usher in a desirable future.
The eight core values which have been mainstreamed in CBC are:
▪ Love
▪ Responsibility
▪ Respect
▪ Unity
▪ Peace
▪ Patriotism
▪ Social Justice
▪ Integrity
Values should be mainstreamed through the whole school approach. Mainstreaming is the
process of identifying suitable opportunities in specific learning areas, where values can be
incorporated in the learning experiences.
PERTINENT AND CONTEMPORARY ISSUES (PCIS)
PCIs are salient issues that have the potential to affect learner’s psychosocial wellbeing,
access to education, retention, transition, completion and ultimately advancement in the
world of work. Education is supposed to equip learners with cognitive and psychosocial
competencies and values necessary in addressing challenges of everyday life.
The PCIs mainstreamed in the learning areas are in four categories:
1. Citizenship: Peace education, Integrity, Ethnic and racial relations, Social cohesion,
Patriotism and Good governance, Child’s rights, Child care and protection.
2. Health Promotion: HIV and AIDS, Alcohol and Substance use, Life style diseases,
personal hygiene, Prevention of Communicable and non communicable diseases,
Menstrual Disorders prevention among others.
3. Life Skills Education, Moral Education and human sexuality Education.
4. Social –economic Issues: Environmental Education, Disaster Risk Reduction ,Safety &
security, radicalization & terrorism prevention education, child care & protection, Gender
and Animal Welfare Education and indigenous knowledge.
18
Link to other subjects/ learning areas
This refers to the relationship between two or more subjects/learning areas. It is a conscious
effort to use learning of concepts in one subject/learning area to relate to learning of concepts
in another subjects/learning area. This requires integration of learning to enable the learner to
make connections across strands and sub strands of different subjects/learning areas. The
teacher should also use related concepts in other subjects/learning areas to reinforce concepts
in the given subjects/learning area. The awareness of linkages between subjects/learning areas
gives an opportunity to borrow and share learning resources in different subjects/learning areas,
thus optimising on available resources.
Suggested Learning Resources
These are any materials, tools and persons that teachers and learners use to facilitate learning
and understanding of concepts. Learning resources make learning real, practical and
pleasurable for the learners.
Suggested Assessment methods
Assessment methods are the strategies and procedures of collecting information to determine
the extent to which learners demonstrate achievement of the specified learning outcomes.
The main purpose of assessing learners is to:
● Inform learning decisions
● Establish the level of learner’s competence
● Ascertain progress against the learning outcomes
● Encourage learners to make judgments about their performance
● Enhance learner motivation
● Identify where intervention, focused support or referral is required
● Make decisions regarding choice of subject, course and careers pathways.
Some of the assessment method include:
● Written assignment
● Observation,
● Oral questioning
● Peer assessment
● Self-assessment
● Project work
Assessment rubric
Learner’s level of performance is described based on the assessment rubrics.
The assessment rubric in the curriculum design has the following
components:

● Four Levels of performance

o Level 3 meeting expectation

a)   determine appropriate class width for grouping data,
Lesson learning outcomes:
By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to;
a) define class widths of grouped data,
